words.definition: A person who chooses to live alone, avoiding company and contact with others.
words.example: After his wife died, he became a recluse, rarely leaving his cabin in the woods.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-close' — someone who keeps re-closing the door on the world.

words.definition: Preferring to stay alone and far away from social contact with other people.
words.example: The reclusive author hadn't given an interview or attended an event in thirty years.
words.mnemonic: Think 'seclusive' — sealed away from society behind closed shutters.

words.definition: Relating to a solitary, secluded life, especially one led for religious reasons.
words.example: The monk embraced an eremitic existence in a remote desert cave, seeing no one for months.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'eremos' (desert) — picture a lone holy man in the empty desert.

words.definition: A person who withdraws from society to live in prayer and religious devotion.
words.example: The medieval anchorite was walled into a small cell beside the church for the rest of her life.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'anchor' — an anchorite anchors to one holy spot, never drifting into society.

words.definition: A member of a religious community who lives together with others under shared rules.
words.example: Unlike the desert hermits, the cenobite shared meals, prayer, and daily chores with his brothers.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'koinos bios' = common life — 'ceno' like 'common,' living life in common.

words.definition: Kept apart from the outside world and its everyday concerns; sheltered and secluded.
words.example: She led a cloistered life on campus, unaware of the turmoil in the wider world.
words.mnemonic: A cloister is a covered monastery walkway — being cloistered means shut inside those walls.

words.definition: To set apart or hide someone or something away from others.
words.example: The judge decided to sequester the jury in a hotel until they reached a verdict.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'quest' — send someone off on a quest, away from everyone.

words.definition: Having a narrow outlook, cut off from and uninterested in other people or ideas.
words.example: Growing up in that insular village, he had never met anyone born in another country.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'insula' = island — an insular person is mentally marooned on their own island.

words.definition: A person who dislikes and distrusts other people in general.
words.example: The old misanthrope chased children off his lawn and slammed the door on carolers.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'miso' (hate) + 'anthropos' (human) — a hater of humans.

words.definition: A general dislike, distrust, or contempt for the human species.
words.example: His misanthropy deepened with age until he trusted no one at all.
words.mnemonic: 'Miso' (hate) + 'anthropy' (humankind) — the condition of hating humankind.

words.definition: A small, exclusive group who share interests and keep outsiders away.
words.example: Only a select coterie of artists was ever invited to the private studio gatherings.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'court-a-ree' — a little royal court of tight-knit insiders.

words.definition: A private or secret meeting of people, often to make an important decision.
words.example: The cardinals gathered in conclave, sealed away, to choose the next pope.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'con' (with) + 'clavis' (key) — locked away 'with a key' to meet in secret.

words.definition: A group of assistants and attendants who travel with an important person.
words.example: The queen swept into the hall followed by her retinue of servants and advisors.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'retain' — the great person retains a crowd of helpers who follow along.

words.definition: The group of attendants and companions who surround an important person.
words.example: The rock star arrived with an entourage of bodyguards, stylists, and hangers-on.
words.mnemonic: French 'entour' means surround — picture the crowd that surrounds a celebrity.

words.definition: A secluded dwelling where someone lives apart from society.
words.example: He retreated to a mountain hermitage to write and pray in total solitude.
words.mnemonic: 'Hermit' + '-age' (place) — the place where a solitary dweller makes a home.

words.definition: The quality of being quiet and unwilling to share one's thoughts or feelings.
words.example: Her reticence during the interview made it hard to know what she truly believed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'reti-CENSE' — picture someone censoring their own words, holding them back before they escape.

words.definition: A shy lack of belief in one's own abilities or worth.
words.example: His diffidence kept him from raising his hand even when he clearly knew the answer.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'fidere' (to trust) + 'dis-' (not) — literally not trusting yourself.

words.definition: A grumpy, ill-tempered person who is stubborn and easily annoyed.
words.example: The old curmudgeon next door yelled at every child who stepped on his lawn.
words.mnemonic: 'Cur' (a mean dog) + 'mudge' — picture a growling dog grumbling in the mud.

words.definition: To deliberately shut someone out of a group or social circle.
words.example: After he broke the team's trust, his teammates began to ostracize him at every practice.
words.mnemonic: Ancient Greeks scratched names on 'ostraca' (pottery shards) to vote someone out of the city.

words.definition: The act of deliberately shutting someone out of a group or community.
words.example: The whistleblower faced total ostracism, eating lunch alone every day after his report.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'ostrakon,' the pottery shard citizens dropped to banish a person from Athens.

words.definition: To reject someone or something with scorn and disdain.
words.example: She spurned his apology, turning away before he could even finish speaking.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spur' — imagine spurring a horse to kick the thing away from you.

words.definition: To refuse an offer or approach in an abrupt, unfriendly way.
words.example: Every time he tried to help, she rebuffed him with a cold, silent stare.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'buff' of wind or a polishing cloth pushing someone back as they approach.

words.definition: A person who is despised and avoided by everyone around them.
words.example: After the scandal, the once-popular banker became a pariah no one would sit beside.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pari-AH!' — picture a crowd gasping 'ah!' and backing away from one lone figure.

words.definition: To formally expel someone from a church or membership in an organization.
words.example: The bishop threatened to excommunicate any priest who openly defied the ruling.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-' (out) + 'commun' — to cut someone completely out of the common fold.

words.definition: To move someone or something to a lower, less important rank or place.
words.example: After a dismal season, the football club was relegated to the second division.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-LEG-ate' — picture something being sent down to the bottom leg of the ladder.

words.definition: To treat a person or group as unimportant and push them to the edges.
words.example: The new policy marginalized older workers, leaving them out of every major decision.
words.mnemonic: Think of the 'margin' of a page — shoved to the blank edge, away from the main text.

words.definition: Cut off from contact with others, unable to send or receive any messages.
words.example: During the silent retreat she went incommunicado, leaving her phone switched off for a week.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) stuck onto 'communicate' — a Spanish-sounding word for total radio silence.

words.definition: Relating to a simple, secluded life devoted to discipline and solitude.
words.example: He lived a monastic existence in a bare room, rising at dawn to read in silence.
words.mnemonic: Comes straight from 'monastery' — picture monks in plain robes living solitary, stripped-down lives.

words.definition: Choosing to abstain from marriage and sexual relationships, often for religious reasons.
words.example: He took a vow to remain celibate when he entered the priesthood.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'cell-i-bait' — imagine living alone in a bare cell, no partner in sight.

words.definition: A warm, cheerful friendliness that puts other people at ease.
words.example: The host's bonhomie filled the room, and soon total strangers were laughing like old friends.
words.mnemonic: French 'bon homme' = 'good man' — picture a beaming, good-natured fellow radiating warmth.

words.definition: To spend time with or associate regularly, especially with people considered disreputable.
words.example: The detective warned him to stop consorting with known criminals if he wanted to stay out of trouble.
words.mnemonic: con- (with) + sort: you sort yourself in WITH a certain SORT of people.

words.definition: To mix socially, especially with those of higher rank or wealth.
words.example: At the gala she hobnobbed with senators and film stars as if she'd known them for years.
words.mnemonic: Hob-NOB: picture rubbing heads (a 'nob' is a knob) with the aristocratic 'nobs' over drinks.

words.definition: To come together into a group or crowd in one place.
words.example: After the alarm, students congregated on the lawn, waiting for permission to re-enter the building.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + greg (flock, as in 'gregarious'): the flock flocks together.

words.definition: To gather people together formally for a meeting or assembly.
words.example: The committee will convene at noon to vote on the proposed budget.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + vene (come, as in 'venue'): everyone comes together at the venue.

words.definition: To gather or cluster into a rounded, disordered mass.
words.example: Over centuries, dust and ice agglomerated into the comet now streaking across our sky.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a glob' + Latin glomus (ball): loose bits clump into a glob.

words.definition: The ordinary people who live in a particular country or area.
words.example: The new tax outraged the populace, and protests soon filled every major square.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'popular place': the mass of common folk filling a place.

words.definition: The whole body of people who legally belong to a nation or state.
words.example: A well-informed citizenry is essential to any functioning democracy.
words.mnemonic: citizen + -ry (a collective ending, like 'peasantry'): all the members lumped into one body.

words.definition: Relating to the middle class, often with conventional, materialistic values.
words.example: He mocked the bourgeois obsession with matching furniture and tidy suburban lawns.
words.mnemonic: From French 'bourg' (town/borough): the town-dwelling merchant middle class.

words.definition: Belonging to the common people, or lacking refinement and cultivation.
words.example: The wine snob dismissed the boxed red as hopelessly plebeian.
words.mnemonic: In ancient Rome the 'plebs' were the common masses, ranked far below the patricians.

words.definition: Belonging to the highest social class; aristocratic and refined.
words.example: Her patrician manners and clipped accent marked her as old-money aristocracy.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'pater' (father): the founding fathers of Rome and their noble descendants.

words.definition: People of high social standing, ranking just below the nobility.
words.example: The country gentry spent their autumns hunting foxes across sprawling estates.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'gentle' and 'genteel' (Latin gens, birth): the well-born, gentle folk.

words.definition: Having a narrow outlook limited to a small local area or concern.
words.example: His parochial views never extended beyond the affairs of his own tiny village.
words.mnemonic: From 'parish': thinking no bigger than your own little church parish.

words.definition: Unsophisticated or narrow, typical of areas far from a cultural capital.
words.example: After a year abroad, she found her hometown's tastes charmingly provincial.
words.mnemonic: From 'province': far from the capital, so rustic and unsophisticated.

words.definition: Familiar with and at ease among many countries and cultures; worldly.
words.example: London's cosmopolitan crowd chattered in a dozen languages over their morning coffee.
words.mnemonic: cosmo (world, as in 'cosmos') + polis (city): a citizen of the whole world.

words.definition: Suave, polished, and courteous in manner, especially in social settings.
words.example: The urbane host moved through the party dispensing witty compliments to every guest.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'urban': the smooth, polished manners of someone raised in the sophisticated city.

words.definition: To formally withdraw membership from an alliance, federation, or larger political body.
words.example: When the council ignored their grievances for years, three northern provinces voted to secede and form their own state.
words.mnemonic: se- (apart) + cede (to go): to 'go apart.' Picture the region saying 'see ya' as it leaves.

words.definition: Having a warm, easygoing friendliness that makes others feel relaxed and welcome.
words.example: They spent the afternoon in companionable silence, each reading while the rain fell outside.
words.mnemonic: Companion + -able: literally 'able to be a good companion' to sit beside.

words.definition: Inclined to stick tightly with one's own group and to keep outsiders at a distance.
words.example: New hires found the veteran staff clannish, sharing lunches and inside jokes no one else was invited into.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clan-ish': acting like a tight Scottish clan that bars anyone not born into it.

words.definition: The philosophical view that only one's own mind is certain to exist.
words.example: His solipsism was so complete that he treated every stranger as a figment with no inner life of their own.
words.mnemonic: Latin solus (alone) + ipse (self): 'alone-self' — only my self is real.

words.definition: Absorbed in oneself to the point of ignoring or doubting that others are real.
words.example: Her solipsistic diary entries recorded only her own moods, as if the war raging outside simply didn't exist.
words.mnemonic: Same root solus + ipse: living as if only your 'sole self' matters.

words.definition: Fearful of or hostile toward people from other countries or cultures.
words.example: The new immigration posters were openly xenophobic, blaming newcomers for every local problem.
words.mnemonic: Greek xenos (stranger) + phobia (fear): fear of strangers.

words.definition: An aggressive, unreasonable belief in the superiority of one's own group or cause.
words.example: His chauvinism showed whenever he insisted no foreign team could ever match his country's players.
words.mnemonic: Named for Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier so fanatically devoted to Napoleon he became a byword for blind loyalty.

words.definition: Rigidly devoted to one faction, often with narrow, divisive hostility toward others.
words.example: Decades of sectarian violence had split the city into neighborhoods that never spoke to one another.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'sect': picture a breakaway sect that scorns everyone outside its walls.

words.definition: Sharply irritable and prone to spiteful, stinging remarks.
words.example: Tired and underslept, she gave a waspish reply that left the intern near tears.
words.mnemonic: A wasp stings sharply and without warning — a waspish person snaps with stinging words.

words.definition: Full of harsh, bitter, and abusive language.
words.example: The critic's vituperative review didn't just pan the film — it mocked the director personally.
words.mnemonic: Latin vituperare, 'to blame': hear 'VILE + uproar-ative' — a vile uproar of insults.

words.definition: A person newly risen to wealth or status but lacking the matching social grace.
words.example: The old families dismissed him as a parvenu whose mansion was grander than his manners.
words.mnemonic: French parvenir, 'to arrive': the newly 'arrived' upstart flaunting fresh money.

words.definition: A person who intrudes into a place or group where they do not belong.
words.example: The regulars fell silent and stared, treating the newcomer at their table like an interloper.
words.mnemonic: inter- (between) + lope (to run in): someone who lopes in between where they weren't invited.

words.definition: A persistent critic who provokes others by annoyingly challenging them.
words.example: As the council's resident gadfly, she stood up at every meeting to question budgets no one else dared to.
words.mnemonic: Literally a biting fly that goads cattle — it buzzes and needles until the herd finally moves.

words.definition: A group of hired or fawning supporters who applaud and cheer on cue.
words.example: The senator traveled with a loyal claque that cheered his every line, drowning out the hecklers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clap': a claque is paid to clap.

words.definition: Marked by friendly cooperation and shared authority among coworkers.
words.example: The department kept a collegial atmosphere, where even junior researchers' ideas were debated as equals.
words.mnemonic: From 'colleague': colleagues working side by side, sharing power as equals.

words.definition: Naturally sociable and pleasant enough to fit easily into any social group.
words.example: With his easy laugh and gift for small talk, he was the most clubbable man at the firm.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'club-able' — the kind of person any club would happily let in.

words.definition: Shy and inclined to withdraw from company or public attention.
words.example: So retiring was she that she slipped out of her own birthday party before the toasts began.
words.mnemonic: Picture someone forever 'retiring' to a quiet back room, away from the noisy crowd.

words.definition: To deliberately avoid or keep away from someone or something.
words.example: After the scandal broke, former friends began to shun him at every gathering.
words.mnemonic: 'Shun' rhymes with 'run' — you run from whatever you shun.

words.definition: To share one's deepest thoughts and feelings in close, quiet exchange.
words.example: She walked alone at dawn to commune with the silent hills and clear her head.
words.mnemonic: 'Communicate' boiled down to something intimate — one soul opening to another.

words.definition: To wander about in search of pleasure or amusement.
words.example: Instead of finishing the report, they gallivanted around Europe on a sudden whim.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gallant' — a knight galloping off on carefree adventures.

words.definition: To feel or express discontent, fretting over what one lacks.
words.example: Rather than repine over the promotion he never got, he quietly started applying elsewhere.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-pine' — to pine again and again, sighing with dissatisfaction.

words.definition: A close fellowship or association of people united by a shared purpose.
words.example: The parish sodality met every Thursday to organize meals for the housebound.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sociality' — a tight-knit society of companions bound together.

words.definition: Nearness in place, time, or kinship.
words.example: Their romance grew almost entirely from propinquity — adjacent desks and shared lunch breaks.
words.mnemonic: 'Prop-in-quity' — being propped right in the vicinity of someone.

words.definition: The surrounding area or the people living nearby.
words.example: News of the barn fire spread through the whole vicinage before sunrise.
words.mnemonic: Cousin of 'vicinity' — the vicinage is simply your neighborhood.

words.definition: A fellow member of a profession or group; a trusted colleague.
words.example: The surgeon quietly consulted a confrere before attempting the risky operation.
words.mnemonic: French 'con' (with) + 'frère' (brother) — a brother-in-arms at work.

words.definition: The custom or practice of eating together at the same table.
words.example: In that village, commensality mattered so much that no one lifted a fork until all were seated.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'com' (together) + 'mensa' (table) — sharing one board.

words.definition: The state of being related by blood or descent from a common ancestor.
words.example: The marriage was forbidden because of the close consanguinity between the two cousins.
words.mnemonic: 'Con' (together) + Latin 'sanguis' (blood) — people who share the same blood.

words.definition: Intimate sharing of thoughts and feelings; deep mutual fellowship.
words.example: Sitting by the fire in easy silence, the old friends felt a quiet communion.
words.mnemonic: 'Common' + 'union' — a union built on what people hold in common.

words.definition: A breakdown of social norms leaving people feeling rootless and without purpose.
words.example: The abandoned factory town sank into anomie once the last jobs vanished.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'a-' (without) + 'nomos' (law) — a condition with no guiding rules.

words.definition: To go to live in or retreat to the countryside.
words.example: Weary of the city's noise, the writer chose to rusticate in a remote stone cottage.
words.mnemonic: Think 'rustic' — turning your life rustic by moving to rural quiet.

words.definition: To keep someone or something away from other people, in a private or isolated place.
words.example: After the scandal, the actor chose to seclude himself in a remote cabin far from reporters.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'see-clude' → to 'exclude' from being seen; shut away where no one can see you.

words.definition: A trusted person with whom one shares private thoughts, feelings, or secrets.
words.example: She told her confidant everything, certain the secret would never leave the room.
words.mnemonic: Root 'confide' + 'ant' → the person you confide in; the one who has your confidence.

description: advanced and low-frequency — solitude and society
